items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="育">bring up</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="育てる">raise</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana make it transitive, so you are the one bringing a child or an animal up.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's little brother feeds his bean sprout fizzy <reading>soda</reading> every morning, and somehow the plant shoots up tall. Feeding and tending a living thing until it grows is how you <vocabulary form="育てる">raise</vocabulary> it, 「<reading>そだてる</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 育（そだ）＋つ.
items.mnemonic_text: Growing on its own: sodatsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="育">bring up</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="育つ">grow up</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana make it intransitive, so the child comes up on its own and no one is raising it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound in 育てる, so the twin where someone simply <vocabulary form="育つ">grows up</vocabulary> on their own is <reading>そだつ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乾（かわ）＋かす.
items.mnemonic_text: Drying a dry (乾) stalk further: kawakasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You hold a soaked towel flat in front of the heater and keep it there until not one drop is left. Forcing all the water out of a wet thing like that is what it is to <vocabulary form="乾かす">dry</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You push your rain-soaked jacket through a <reading>car wash</reading>, and it comes out the far end with every drop blasted off. Driving the water out of a wet thing is how you <vocabulary form="乾かす">dry</vocabulary> it, 「<reading>かわかす</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乾（かわ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Becoming dry on its own: kawaku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You peg the washing out in the midday sun and come back to sheets that are stiff, warm, and holding no water at all. A thing losing every drop on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="乾く">dry</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 乾かす, so the twin where something goes <vocabulary form="乾く">dry</vocabulary> on its own, with no heater on it, is <reading>かわく</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 濡（ぬ）＋らす.
items.mnemonic_text: Making something wet on purpose: nurasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You tip a full watering can straight over the folded picnic blanket until it is soaked through and heavy. Pouring water onto a thing until it is soaked is what it is to <vocabulary form="濡らす">wet</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>gnu</reading> at the riverbank keeps flicking water over its back with its horns until the whole herd stands there dripping. Splashing water onto something until it drips is how you <vocabulary form="濡らす">wet</vocabulary> it, 「<reading>ぬらす</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 濡（ぬ）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: Getting wet by chance: nureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sky opens while you are still ten minutes from home with no umbrella, and by the corner your shirt is stuck to your back. Rain landing on you until you are soaked is what it is to <vocabulary form="濡れる">get wet</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 濡らす, so the twin where you end up <vocabulary form="濡れる">wet</vocabulary> with no say in it is <reading>ぬれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 沸（わ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Water bubbling up on its own: waku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the kettle on a high flame and wait until the surface is rolling over and throwing off steam. Water climbing to that churn on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="沸く">boil</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi fills a steel <reading>wok</reading> with water on the konbini hotplate, and soon it is heaving and spitting all by itself. Water going wild with heat like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="沸く">boil</vocabulary>, 「<reading>わく</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 沸（わ）＋かす.
items.mnemonic_text: Heating water until it boils: wakasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stand over the pot with the gas turned up full, holding the water on the heat until it roars. Driving water up to a rolling churn yourself is what it is to <vocabulary form="沸かす">boil</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 沸く, so the twin where you are the one heating the water up to a churn is <reading>わかす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="沸かす">boil</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 燃（も）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: Fire catching on its own: moeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A dropped match catches the dry grass at the field's edge, and the whole slope is orange before anyone can stand up. Something going up in flame on its own is what it is to <vocabulary form="燃える">burn</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>mower</reading> on Sei's school field throws a spark into the heap of dry cuttings, and the pile is alight in seconds. Stuff catching and climbing into flame is what it means to <vocabulary form="燃える">burn</vocabulary>, 「<reading>もえる</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 燃（も）＋やす.
items.mnemonic_text: Setting fire to something: moyasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You rake the fallen leaves into a heap in the yard, hold a lighter to one edge, and step back as it takes. Setting a thing alight on purpose is what it is to <vocabulary form="燃やす">burn</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 燃える, so the twin where you are the one lighting the fire is <reading>もやす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="燃やす">burn</vocabulary> something.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 沈（しず）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: Water swallowing something down: shizumu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A slow leak fills the rowboat until it tips its nose down and slides under the lake, and the water closes flat over the top. A heavy thing dropping below the surface and staying there is what it is to <vocabulary form="沈む">sink</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The free diver breathes out, whispers 「<reading>she zooms</reading>」, and drops straight down to the dark lake bed. Going under the water and staying down there is what it means to <vocabulary form="沈む">sink</vocabulary>, 「<reading>しずむ</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 浮（う）＋かぶ.
items.mnemonic_text: Bobbing lightly on the water: ukabu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You let go of the beach ball under the pool water and it shoots straight back up to sit on the surface. A thing riding on top of the water instead of going under is what it is to <vocabulary form="浮かぶ">float</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You <reading>hook a boot</reading> out of the canal, and it will not stay under no matter how you shove it. It keeps riding back up to the top, and sitting on the surface like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="浮かぶ">float</vocabulary>, 「<reading>うかぶ</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 流（なが）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: Water running its course: nagareru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="流">current</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="流れる">flow</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana just make it a verb, water carrying itself along with nobody pushing it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The river guide never stops talking, keeping up one long <reading>nagging rule</reading> about life jackets while the raft is swept on with no paddling. Water carrying things along on its own is what it means to <vocabulary form="流れる">flow</vocabulary>, 「<reading>ながれる</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 流（なが）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Letting the water run: nagasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="流">current</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="流す">let flow</vocabulary> word are the same. The trailing kana make it the one you do to something, so you send the water on its way yourself.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 流れる, so the twin where you set the water moving yourself is <reading>ながす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="流す">let flow</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 回（まわ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Spinning around a loop: mawaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A wheel jolts loose from the cart and rolls off on its own, going <kanji form="回">round</kanji> and round all the way down the hill. Something spinning in circles by itself is what it is to <vocabulary form="回る">turn</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei drops a <reading>marble</reading> into a big funnel and it races around and around the inside wall before it finally drops through. Going round a circle over and over like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="回る">turn</vocabulary>, 「<reading>まわる</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 回（まわ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Turning something by hand: mawasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You grab the stiff crank on the well and force it <kanji form="回">round</kanji>, one hard shove after another, until the bucket starts to rise. Driving a thing in a circle with your own hand is what it is to <vocabulary form="回す">turn</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know this sound from 回る, so the twin where your hand is the thing spinning it is <reading>まわす</reading>, to <vocabulary form="回す">turn</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 引（ひ）＋っ＋越（こ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Pulling your life over a hill: hikkosu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> every box, every stick of furniture, and your whole life out of one apartment and cart it across town to the next. Dragging your entire household to a new address is what it is to <vocabulary form="引っ越す">move</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 通（かよ）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: Passing the same road daily: kayou.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Slip into the <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> that pours down one road every morning and back every night. Making that same trip over and over, day after day, is what it means <vocabulary form="通う">to commute</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every dawn the station guard sees the same tired man and sighs, <reading>Kai, you</reading> again. Kai rides the same train to the same desk daily, and that worn daily trip is 「<reading>かよう</reading>」, <vocabulary form="通う">to commute</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 通（とお）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Going straight through a road: tooru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary> word are the same word. With this ending it just means something moves along the road and out the far side on its own, with nobody pushing it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>toll</reading>-gate guard lifts the barrier for one more truck and it rolls straight past him into the dark. A thing that goes in one side of a gap and out the far side on its own is 「<reading>とおる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 通（とお）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Letting something pass through: toosu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="通す">to let pass</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending adds a hand on the gate, so someone now moves the traffic through instead of it flowing past on its own.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 通 sounds like とお from 通る, so the hands-on version, <vocabulary form="通す">to let pass</vocabulary>, is just <reading>とおす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 凍（こお）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Ice locking the water still: kooru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Leave water still in the cold long enough and it turns hard and <kanji form="凍">frozen</kanji> all by itself. Water going solid like that, with nobody freezing it, is <vocabulary form="凍る">to freeze</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the garden pond a girl named <reading>Cora</reading> leaves her hose in the water overnight, and by dawn it sits locked in a clear block she cannot bend. Water setting hard and still on its own like that is 「<reading>こおる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="凍る">to freeze</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 溶（と）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: A shape softening away in water: tokeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Drop a sugar cube into hot tea and stir once. It loses its edges, goes cloudy, and spreads through the water until it is gone, and that is what <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary> looks like.
items.reading_mnemonic: A chocolate coin left on the sunny windowsill goes from a hard <reading>token</reading> to a brown smear across the paint by noon. Something firm turning soft and runny with nobody touching it is 「<reading>とける</reading>」, <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 腐（くさ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Flesh (肉) crumbling under a roof: kusaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Shove a tub of rice to the back of the fridge and forget it for three weeks. The smell hits before you see the domed, slimy lid, and food left to turn that far is what <vocabulary form="腐る">to rot / spoil</vocabulary> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: A bowl of <reading>couscous</reading> left on the counter through a hot week goes grey, then furry, then sharp enough to drive everyone out of the kitchen. Food breaking down on its own like that is 「<reading>くさる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="腐る">to rot / spoil</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 逃（に）＋げる.
items.mnemonic_text: Slipping off the road: nigeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The side door is propped open a crack, and by the time the guard turns back the cell is empty. Getting clear through a gap before anyone can stop you is what it means <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Nigel</reading> the gerbil works a bar of his cage loose every night and is halfway down the hall before the lights come on. A small thing bolting for the gap the moment it opens is 「<reading>にげる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 追（お）＋いかける.
items.mnemonic_text: Following closely on the road: oikakeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A bun rolls off the bakery shelf and a boy runs after it down three aisles, hands out, never quite closing the gap. Staying right behind a thing that will not stop, trying to catch it, is what it means <vocabulary form="追いかける">to chase</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The keeper yells <reading>oi</reading> as a <reading>cackling</reading> hyena tears after the loose goat, staying one stride off its tail the whole length of the pen. That noisy pursuit, right behind and never letting up, is 「<reading>おいかける</reading>」, <vocabulary form="追いかける">to chase</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 断（ことわ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Cutting off a request: kotowaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The host holds out the good sweets and you put a flat hand over your cup and say no until she takes the plate back. Turning down what someone offers, out loud and on purpose, is what it means <vocabulary form="断る">to refuse / decline</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Offered a pillow of <reading>cotton wool</reading> for the long ride, the old man shakes his head and sits bolt upright for four hours instead. Pushing back a thing you are handed, plainly and on purpose, is 「<reading>ことわる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="断る">to refuse / decline</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 頼（たの）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: Trusting your weight to a bundle: tanomu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You catch your neighbour at the gate, hold out your spare key, and ask her to feed the cat while you are gone. Putting a task in someone else's hands and counting on them to do it is what it means <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you feed the lone vending machine your last coins and say <reading>ta</reading> before it even answers. It only hums, so you ask again, staking the whole climb on that one machine working, and that is 「<reading>たのむ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 助（たす）＋かる.
items.mnemonic_text: Getting rescued on your own: tasukaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="助">help</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending flips it around so the help lands on you, and you are the one pulled clear, not the one doing the pulling.
items.reading_mnemonic: You go through the ice at the riverbank and a walrus hooks both <reading>tusks</reading> under your arms and heaves you onto the bank. Being lifted clear by something outside you, with no effort of your own, is 「<reading>たすかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 助（たす）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: Lending strength (力) to someone: tasukeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="助">help</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="助ける">to help / rescue</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending points it outward, so you are the one reaching in and pulling someone else clear.
items.reading_mnemonic: You met this sound as たす in 助かる, so the outward version, <vocabulary form="助ける">to help / rescue</vocabulary>, is simply <reading>たすける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 叱（しか）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) baring teeth (七): to scold.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A kid tips a full tray of paint across the floor, and the teacher kneels down and tells him in a hard, flat voice that this was not okay. Speaking to someone that sharply about what they did wrong is what it means <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each wrong answer earns one more tap of <reading>chalk</reading> on the desk while the teacher lists your mistakes in a rising voice. That steady, sharp correction for a fault is 「<reading>しかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 褒（ほ）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: Clothing (衤) draped in honor: homeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your kid brings home a drawing, and you pin it on the fridge, point to the careful shading, and tell her it is genuinely good. Saying plainly to someone that what they made is good is how you <vocabulary form="褒める">praise</vocabulary> them.
items.reading_mnemonic: A small kid on the little-league team finally connects and puts one over the fence, and the whole bench swarms him for the <reading>home run</reading>. Loading that kind of open approval onto someone for a job well done is 「<reading>ほめる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="褒める">to praise</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 謝（あやま）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Words (言) offered like thanks: ayamaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You back your bike into a parked car, wince at the fresh scratch, and go knock on the owner's door to say sorry and offer to pay. Owning that you did wrong and saying so to the person is what it means <vocabulary form="謝る">to apologize</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>A llama</reading> at the petting zoo spits across the fence onto a boy's jacket, then drops its head and shuffles as if it knows it went too far. Admitting a wrong to the person you wronged, out loud, is 「<reading>あやまる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="謝る">to apologize</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 喜（よろこ）＋ぶ.
items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) opening wide in joy: yorokobu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand someone the news they have been hoping for and watch them <kanji form="喜">rejoice</kanji>, all grin and thank-yous and a little bounce. That whole warm rush when something goes right for you is being <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">pleased</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi slides <reading>your cocoa</reading> across the konbini counter on the cold morning you needed it most, and you light up before it lands. That instant lift when a good thing reaches your hands is 「<reading>よろこぶ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">to be pleased</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 怒（おこ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: A heart (心) enslaved (奴) by rage: okoru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone slides into the parking spot you waited ten minutes for and smirks at you through the glass. Your face goes hot, your voice climbs, and that sudden flare of temper is what it means <vocabulary form="怒る">to get angry</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: One slice of slippery <reading>okra</reading> slides across your plate into the rice, and that alone is enough to tighten your jaw and ruin the meal. Heat rising in you over something that small is 「<reading>おこる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="怒る">to get angry</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 悩（なや）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: A heart (忄) tangled in brains (脳): nayamu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You have two job offers and one week to pick, and every night you lie awake running the same lists. Turning a hard choice over and over until it wears a groove in you is <vocabulary form="悩む">to worry / agonize</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Facing a call he cannot make, the man sits on the step and <reading>gnaws a yam</reading> raw, one slow bite at a time, staring at nothing. Working at a problem that will not come loose like that is 「<reading>なやむ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="悩む">to worry / agonize</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 驚（おどろ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: A horse (馬) rearing up: odoroku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You lift a plant pot to move it and the whole underside is crawling with woodlice spilling out at once. The jump in your chest and the step back you take before you can think is being <vocabulary form="驚く">surprised</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You tip up what looks like an <reading>odd rock</reading> by the step and it opens into a crab and runs across your foot. You are standing before you have decided to move, and that jolt at a thing you did not expect is 「<reading>おどろく</reading>」, <vocabulary form="驚く">to be surprised</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 嘆（なげ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) sighing hard: nageku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: After the storm the old farmer stands in the flattened field and says the same low words about the lost year, over and over, to no one. Letting that grief out loud like that is what it means <vocabulary form="嘆く">to lament</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>A gecko</reading> on the shrine wall lets out a long, creaking wail every dusk over the moths it can no longer reach. Crying that kind of grief openly into the air is 「<reading>なげく</reading>」, <vocabulary form="嘆く">to lament</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 頑（がん）on'yomi ＋ 張（ば）kun'yomi ＋ る.
items.mnemonic_text: Stubbornly (頑) stretching (張) onward: ganbaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To be <kanji form="頑">stubborn</kanji> about how far you can <kanji form="張">stretch</kanji> yourself, and then hold that stretch when it burns, is to <vocabulary form="頑張る">try hard</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 慣（な）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: A heart (忄) settling into a pattern: nareru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Do the same small thing every day and the odd feeling fades on its own. Once it is completely gone, you have <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>nurse</reading> barely reacts to the sight of blood any more. Years on the ward mean she has completely <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it, and that flat shrug is <reading>なれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 経（た）＋つ.
items.mnemonic_text: Time threading through the loom: tatsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="経">pass through</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="経つ">for time to pass</vocabulary> word are the same; the extra kana on the end just makes it something time does by itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a hiker misses the last bus and <reading>tuts</reading> at his watch while the daylight fades. Each tut marks another minute <vocabulary form="経つ">passing</vocabulary> with nothing to fill it, and that slow drip is <reading>たつ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 過（す）＋ぎる.
items.mnemonic_text: A road (辶) going past a fold: sugiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that slides past the mark it was meant to stop at, and keeps sliding, has <vocabulary form="過ぎる">passed or exceeded</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi keeps tipping <reading>sugar</reading> into one coffee and will not stop at two spoons or at ten. The level <vocabulary form="過ぎる">passes</vocabulary> every sane limit, and that pour that never quits is <reading>すぎる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 過（す）＋ごす.
items.mnemonic_text: Letting time pass by choice: sugosu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To let a whole afternoon <kanji form="過">go beyond</kanji> you on purpose, filling every hour of it, is to <vocabulary form="過ごす">spend</vocabulary> that time.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 過ぎる, so its near-twin <vocabulary form="過ごす">to spend time</vocabulary> is simply <reading>すごす</reading>.

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 期（き）＋待（たい）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A period (期) awaited (待): to expect.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji form="待">wait</kanji> out a fixed <kanji form="期">period</kanji>, sure the thing is coming, is to <vocabulary form="期待する">expect</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 願（ねが）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: A head bowed asking a favor: negau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Press your palms together and name aloud the one thing you want another person to grant you. That spoken hope is to <vocabulary form="願う">wish</vocabulary> or request something.
items.reading_mnemonic: The polite お願いします already gave you this reading, so plain <vocabulary form="願う">to wish or request</vocabulary> is <reading>ねがう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 祈（いの）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: An altar (示) plus an axe-shaped vow: inoru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Bow your head, close your eyes, and quietly ask a power you cannot see to keep someone safe. That asking, with nothing but words, is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At dawn a line of pilgrims kneels in one long <reading>row</reading> on the shrine steps, foreheads to the stone, each asking an unseen power for rain. Kneeling in a <reading>row</reading> and begging like that is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いのる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 祝（いわ）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: An altar (示) blessing an event: iwau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Good news lands, so you deliberately gather people, food and noise around the one it happened to. That staged happiness is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The team wins and Sei's whole class erupts, caps in the air, everyone shouting 'I <reading>wow</reading>' around a cake nobody planned. Making that much noise on purpose for one person is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いわう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 祝（しゅく）＋福（ふく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A celebration (祝) of fortune (福): a blessing.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Words that <kanji form="祝">celebrate</kanji> someone while wishing them good fortune are a <vocabulary form="祝福">blessing</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 感（かん）＋謝（しゃ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Feeling (感) thanks (謝): to appreciate.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">feeling</kanji> that wells up and makes you want to <kanji form="謝">thank</kanji> someone to their face is being <vocabulary form="感謝する">grateful</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 間（ま）＋違（ちが）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The space (間) gone wrong (違): a mistake.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>space between</kanji> two pigeonhole dividers is a mail slot, and you shove your letter into the one that <kanji>differs</kanji> from yours by a single room number. Feeding that wrong slot is what it means to <vocabulary>make a mistake</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 間（ま）＋違（ちが）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: Falling into the wrong gap: machigau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji form="間">gap between</kanji> what you believe and what is true turns out to <kanji form="違">differ</kanji>, you are <vocabulary form="間違う">mistaken</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 修（しゅう）＋理（り）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Cultivating (修) the logic (理) back: to repair.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="修">discipline</kanji> a broken machine part by part until every piece lines up with its own <kanji form="理">logic</kanji> again, and that is to <vocabulary form="修理する">repair</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 掛（か）＋かる.
items.mnemonic_text: Hanging in the balance: kakaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A coat on a hook stays put with no one holding it, and an hour spent on a job slips by the same way. Either one just <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> there and takes the time it takes.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leave a taxi parked with its meter on and the fare climbs by itself; the longer the <reading>car</reading> waits, the more it owes. That cost stacking up with no one touching it is for something to <vocabulary form="掛かる">take</vocabulary>, and it is <reading>かかる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 掛（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: Hanging something up: kakeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach up and set the frame on the nail yourself; you choose to put a full hour into the work. Doing either by your own hand is to <vocabulary form="掛ける">hang</vocabulary> a thing or spend the time on it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 掛かる, so its hands-on twin <vocabulary form="掛ける">to hang or spend</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋なる.
items.mnemonic_text: Heavy loads stacking themselves: kasanaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Loose sheets keep drifting down onto each other with no hand guiding them, and the stack grows <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> as each one lands. Left to themselves they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> and settle into a pile.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dancer clacks her <reading>castanets</reading>, and the beats stack so fast they land on top of one another with no gap between them. Sounds falling onto sounds like that is to <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary>, or <reading>かさなる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 重（かさ）＋ねる.
items.mnemonic_text: Stacking heavy loads on purpose: kasaneru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set plate on plate by hand, squaring each one on the last, every <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> disc pushing the stack down harder. Doing it on purpose like that is to <vocabulary form="重ねる">pile up</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 重なる, so its by-hand partner <vocabulary form="重ねる">to pile things up</vocabulary> is simply <reading>かさねる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 知（し）＋らせる.
items.mnemonic_text: Making someone know: shiraseru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>know</kanji> a fact the moment your arrow thuds into the target. Firing that same fact into someone else's target is <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> them.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already learned 知 is 「し」 back in 知る, so <vocabulary>to inform / notify</vocabulary> someone is just <reading>しらせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 届（とど）＋け＋出（で）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Delivering a notice out: todokederu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="届">deliver</kanji> a completed form to the city office and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your hands for good; that is to <vocabulary form="届け出る">report</vocabulary> or file something officially.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 信（しん）＋じる.
items.mnemonic_text: A person's word (言) trusted: shinjiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To take another person's word as plain <kanji form="信">truth</kanji>, with no proof in your hand, is to <vocabulary form="信じる">believe</vocabulary> them.

items.word_type: ichidan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 感（かん）＋じる.
items.mnemonic_text: The heart's field stirred: kanjiru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="感">emotion</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="感じる">to feel</vocabulary> word are the same; the added kana just turns that emotion into something you actively do.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 提（てい）＋出（しゅつ）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Presenting (提) and putting out (出): to submit.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The finished report stays in your hands until you <kanji form="提">carry</kanji> it to the front desk and let it <kanji form="出">leave</kanji> your fingers onto the tray. Letting a document exit you and stay with the office is how you <vocabulary form="提出する">submit</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 申（もう）＋し＋込（こ）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: Speaking your request into the pile: moushikomu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You fill in your name and push the sheet into the <kanji form="込">crowded</kanji> stack of everyone else's forms on the counter. Adding yourself to that packed pile is how you <vocabulary form="申し込む">apply</vocabulary> for a place.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 申（もう）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A humble mouth speaking upward: mousu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You bend low and aim your words at the floor near an important person's feet, so they reach that person from below. Speaking from down there, kept small on purpose, is to <vocabulary form="申す">say something humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny office <reading>mouse</reading> stands at the boardroom table and reports the figures in a voice so meek the directors lean right in. That head-down way of getting a word out is <vocabulary form="申す">to say something, humbly</vocabulary>, and it squeaks out as <reading>もうす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 致（いた）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A humble hand reaching to serve: itasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A servant finishes every task before anyone notices it needed doing, then sweeps away their own footprints so no one sees the work. Getting the whole job done while keeping yourself invisible is to <vocabulary form="致す">do it, humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Two overalled helpers answer every call at the back door with a soft <reading>it's us</reading>, then quietly fix whatever broke and slip out again. Doing the work for someone while staying that far in the background is <vocabulary form="致す">to do, humbly</vocabulary>, spoken as <reading>いたす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 参（まい）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Bowing low on the way: mairu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the car at the gate and walk the last stretch up to the house on foot, hat held in both hands. Coming toward someone that plainly, on foot and uncovered, is to <vocabulary form="参る">come to them humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: An old retainer waves away every offer of a ride, saying that walking to you in person is <reading>my rule</reading>, and sets off down the full length of the road. That slow arrival on your own two feet is <vocabulary form="参る">to go and come humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>まいる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 伺（うかが）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: A person (亻) watching (司) respectfully: ukagau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You knock softly and wait outside the doorway until someone waves you in, then lean your head through to put your question. Approaching a person's home and their attention that carefully is to <vocabulary form="伺う">visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A polite <reading>kangaroo</reading> props its paws on the garden fence and waits to be waved through before hopping in to ask after your health. Peeking in and raising a question that gently is <vocabulary form="伺う">to visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>, which comes out as <reading>うかがう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 拝（はい）＋見（けん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Bowing (拝) to view (見): to humbly look.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You bow so low over the offered document that your <kanji form="見">seeing</kanji> eye has to peer up at it from just above the floor. Looking at what someone shows you from that far down is how you <vocabulary form="拝見する">see it, humbly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — ご＋覧（らん）＋になる.
items.mnemonic_text: Honorific viewing: goran ni naru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the photo album on a stand and step back with folded hands, offering it up the way a gallery presents its finest piece. Letting an honored person <vocabulary form="ご覧になる">see something, honorifically</vocabulary>, means presenting it to them like that.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 召（め）＋し＋上（あ）＋がる.
items.mnemonic_text: Calling something up to eat: meshiagaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored guest never fetches their own meal: the dishes are <kanji form="召">called for</kanji> from the kitchen and carried <kanji form="上">up</kanji> to the head of the table. Eating and drinking what has been summoned and raised to you is to <vocabulary form="召し上がる">eat or drink, honorifically</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The all-purpose respectful verb: irassharu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The white-gloved <reading>usher</reading> at the theatre glides over to walk each important guest in, out, and to their seat without a wasted step. That smooth, honored coming and going is <vocabulary form="いらっしゃる">to be, go, or come, honorifically</vocabulary>, and it sounds like <reading>いらっしゃる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to speak: ossharu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Whatever slow <reading>oh, sure</reading> the old retired professor mutters from his armchair, the whole class copies into their notes as settled fact. Giving a statement that weight because of who spoke it is <vocabulary form="おっしゃる">to say, honorifically</vocabulary>, and the sound is <reading>おっしゃる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The respectful way to do: nasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the grand duchess Nessa decides a thing will happen, it happens — <reading>Nessa rules</reading> the whole estate, and whatever task she takes on, she personally <vocabulary form="なさる">does the action, honorifically</vocabulary>. The sound of that lands as <reading>なさる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — ご＋存（ぞん）＋じ.
items.mnemonic_text: Respectfully preserving knowledge: gozonji.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A fact your honored guest is already <kanji form="存">aware of</kanji> was sitting in their head before you spoke. Something that already <kanji form="存">exists</kanji> in a superior's mind before it is said is the honored form of <vocabulary form="ご存じ">knowing</vocabulary> it.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 頂（いただ）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving something atop your head: itadaku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You take the gift in both hands and lift it up past your forehead, putting yourself lower than the thing you were just given. Receiving or eating anything from that bowed-under position is to <vocabulary form="頂く">receive it, humbly</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine a tame duck waddles up and drops a rice cracker into your cupped hands, and you bow lower than the bird to take it. That <reading>eat a duck</reading> moment, receiving with your head down, is <vocabulary form="頂く">to receive and eat, humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>いただく</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 差（さ）on'yomi ＋ し ＋ 上（あ）kun'yomi ＋ げ ＋ る.
items.mnemonic_text: Offering something up respectfully: sashiageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Noticing the <kanji form="差">difference</kanji> in rank between you and the higher-ranked person, you raise the gift <kanji form="上">up</kanji> with both arms so it travels toward them. Handing something upward across that gap is to <vocabulary form="差し上げる">give, humbly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 下（くだ）＋さる.
items.mnemonic_text: Graciously handing something down: kudasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 承（しょう）＋知（ち）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving (承) knowledge (知) humbly: shouchi suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An order comes in and lands dead center, the way the arrow thumps into the target: now you <kanji form="知">know</kanji> it. Bowing to show it struck home and you will carry it out is how you <vocabulary form="承知する">acknowledge an instruction, humbly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋せる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hanasu: able to speak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the nonstop <kanji form="話">talker</kanji> with the wagging tongue an open microphone and the words just pour out, no gap anywhere. Being able to let language run like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="話せる">be able to speak</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 話 is read 「はな」 from 話す, so <vocabulary form="話せる">can speak</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>はなせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kaku: able to write.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. The added ending only shifts it from doing the writing to being able to do it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is read 「か」 from 書く, so <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>かける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 読（よ）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of yomu: able to read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="読">read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same meaning. The extra ending just moves it from reading to being able to read.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 読 is read 「よ」 from 読む, so <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>よめる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 使（つか）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of tsukau: usable.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new happens here: the <kanji form="使">use</kanji> kanji you already know is exactly what <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 「つか」 in 使う, so <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> just wears that same reading with a new tail: <reading>つかえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of iku: able to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji stands on its own here, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> is that same kanji and not one idea more.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「い」 in this word is the one from 行く that you already know, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>いける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 来（こ）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kuru: able to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
items.reading_mnemonic: Once the runaway goat is <reading>collared</reading> and leashed, it <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> to you from right across the field. A goat you can call back in like that is <reading>こられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べられる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of taberu: able to eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji does all the work on its own here, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> means just what that character has always meant.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「た」 is the same one 食べる taught you earlier, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> is simply <reading>たべられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 飲（の）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of nomu: able to drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: No story to build here: the <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> kanji is the whole word, and <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> means the very same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You know 「の」 already from 飲む, so <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> follows straight on as <reading>のめる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of miru: able to see.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="見">see</kanji> kanji does not change when it becomes a word, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> is simply the character you have already met.
items.reading_mnemonic: This 「み」 is the reading you picked up in 見る, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>みられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋来（き）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Kanji form of dekiru: to be possible.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once every part has <kanji form="来">come</kanji> in, a finished thing <kanji form="出">exits</kanji> the far end of the line. That finished thing is proof the whole job was <vocabulary form="出来る">possible</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泳（およ）＋げる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of oyogu: able to swim.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Step off the riverbank into deep water and you do not go under; your limbs already know the strokes. Holding yourself up and moving through the water on your own is what it means that you <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「およ」 from 泳ぐ, so <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>およげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 走（はし）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hashiru: able to run.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Same character, same meaning: the <kanji form="走">run</kanji> kanji you already know is all there is to <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「はし」 here is the same one from 走る, so <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary> reads as <reading>はしれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 会（あ）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of au: able to meet.
items.meaning_mnemonic: There is nothing extra to learn here, since the <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> point at exactly the same idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already say 「あ」 this way in 会う, so <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> is nothing more than <reading>あえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 買（か）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kau: able to buy.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="買">buy</kanji> kanji carries straight over into this word, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> holds no meaning the kanji did not already.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「か」 is the reading 買う already gave you, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> lands as <reading>かえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乗（の）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of noru: able to ride.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This word adds nothing to its kanji: <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> is the <kanji form="乗">ride</kanji> kanji you have already met, unchanged.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「の」 in this word comes straight from 乗る, so <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>のれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋かせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of iku: making someone go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At its core this word is still the <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji. The tail added on means you <vocabulary form="行かせる">make or let someone go</vocabulary>, whether they want to or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same 「い」 as in 行く, so <vocabulary form="行かせる">to make/let go</vocabulary> keeps that opening sound and becomes <reading>いかせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べさせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of taberu: making someone eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Underneath, this is only the <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji again. The extra endings shift it to mean you <vocabulary form="食べさせる">make or let another person eat</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「た」 is the one 食べる gave you, so <vocabulary form="食べさせる">to make/let eat</vocabulary> starts the same and runs on to <reading>たべさせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of yaru: making someone do it.

items.reading_mnemonic: You learned 「ま」 back in 待つ, so the drawn-out <vocabulary form="待たされる">to be made to wait</vocabulary> is still just <reading>またされる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 叱（しか）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of shikaru: on the receiving end of a scolding.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Knock a jar off Grandma Kane's shelf and every cat goes still while she turns and scolds you in a long, rising voice. Standing there and taking all of it is what it means <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「しか」 from 叱る, so the version done to you, <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>, is <reading>しかられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 褒（ほ）＋められる.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand a drawing to the teacher and she holds it up to the whole class, naming every good line in it. Having your work lifted up for the whole room to see is what it means <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「ほ」 from 褒める, so the same thing coming back at you, <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>, is <reading>ほめられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泣（な）＋かれる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of naku: suffering from someone's crying.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The person beside you suddenly bursts out <kanji form="泣">crying</kanji>, and now their misery is your problem to deal with. Being left holding someone else's tears like that is being <vocabulary form="泣かれる">cried at</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「な」 from 泣く, so that same crying aimed at you, <vocabulary form="泣かれる">to be cried at (adversity)</vocabulary>, is <reading>なかれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A blow (殳) striking down: to kill.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower and the motor goes quiet for good under your hands. Ending a running thing on purpose like that is what it means <vocabulary form="殺す">to kill</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The frog <reading>chorus</reading> at the riverbank drones so flat and so long that it could <vocabulary form="殺す">kill</vocabulary> every houseplant on the windowsill. A sound that deadly is <reading>ころす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋される.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of korosu: to be killed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A beetle wanders onto the train track at exactly the wrong second. The 8:15 does not slow down, and being the one it happens to is <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 殺 is 「ころ」 from 殺す, the verb you first met it in, so <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary> is <reading>ころされる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Climbing out over the box rim is only the <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>. Once your feet hit the road and you keep walking, that is <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 出 is 「で」 from 出る, the verb it first showed up in, so <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary> is <reading>でかける</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持ち) and returning (帰る): to take away.
